sec.title: Background
sec.p: Frailty is highly prevalent among older gastric cancer patients and strongly associated with adverse postoperative outcomes. While frailty interventions have been implemented, few have focused on family cohesion as a pivotal aspect. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of a family cohesion-centered frailty intervention grounded in the Satir Family Therapy Model among for high-risk frailty older patients with gastric cancer.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A non-randomized, time-based controlled trial was conducted in a tertiary hospital in China, with 79 participants and their family caregivers allocated according to sequential admission periods into an experimental group (n = 40) or a control group (n = 39). The intervention focused on enhancing family communication and cohesion. Frailty, family cohesion, self-efficacy, anxiety, depression, and quality of life were assessed on the day of admission (T0), at the end of the intervention, specifically at 4 weeks after surgery (T1), and 1 month after the completion of the intervention (T2). Analyses used generalized estimating equations with multiple imputation under an intention-to-treat framework, adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates. Moderation analyses tested three-way interactions.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Significant group by time interactions were observed for frailty, family cohesion, self-efficacy, anxiety, depression, and quality of life (all P < 0.05). Compared with usual care, the experimental group showed greater reductions in frailty, anxiety, and depression and was associated with improvement in family cohesion, self-efficacy, and quality of life, with effects strengthening at T2. Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent results. Limited moderating effects were identified for age, education, and TNM stage.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The family-cohesion-centered intervention was associated with multidimensional and sustained improvements among older gastric cancer patients at high risk of frailty. By integrating the Satir Family Therapy Model into perioperative care, this program may represent a feasible family-based approach that could contribute to optimizing frailty management and postoperative recovery. However, the non-randomized, time-based controlled design may introduce potential biases, including from secular trends or contamination; such biases could affect the estimates in either direction. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to verify this.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: According to the most recent global cancer data, the incidence rate and mortality of gastric cancer are both in fifth place among malignant tumors [1, 2]. The survival period of gastric cancer patients has gradually extended due to the advancement of cancer diagnosis and treatment technology. Older patients with gastric cancer account for 72.8% of all gastric cancer patients [3]. The incidence rate of frailty in older patients with gastric cancer is as high as 45.9% due to the abnormal nutrition metabolism of gastric cancer itself, combined with the influence of surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy [4–6]. Frailty represents a complex age-related syndrome characterized by decreased multi-organ system function, reduced physiological reserves, and increased susceptibility to various stressors. It is gradually becoming one of the determining factors affecting the prognosis of older patients with gastric cancer [7–9].

The development of frailty exhibits continuity and dynamism, and changes in the group are heterogeneous. In the early stage, our research team constructed a latent growth mixed model by collecting 1-year follow-up data of older patients with gastric cancer, identifying three trajectories of frailty and their relationship with health outcomes [10]. In addition, a predictive model was developed, employing an online nomogram [11], thereby providing a scalable instrument for the identification of high-risk frailty patients. The decline trajectory of older patients with gastric cancer varies, and their impact on prognosis differs significantly, thereby greatly increasing the burden of care. Consequently, older patients diagnosed with gastric cancer should be regarded as a priority population for frailty management. The identification of high-risk populations based on frailty heterogeneity trajectories and the implementation of specific interventions can facilitate early preoperative risk stratification, improve the efficiency of medical resource allocation and utilization, and alleviate physical, psychological, and social functional barriers caused by disease and treatment.

In recent years, frailty interventions for older patients with gastric cancer have primarily centered on individual behavioral aspects, including nutritional support, exercise, and multimodal pre-rehabilitation [12]. The survival period of older patients with gastric cancer has been continuously increasing, which has resulted in a gradual transition of their treatment environment from hospitals to their homes. The family, as the most fundamental social unit, has emerged as the primary locus for older patients with gastric cancer to enhance their physical strength and well-being [13–15]. Research showed that a lack of family support had a harmful effect on frailty in older adults [16]. Consequently, it is important to explore the prognostic implications of family-centered frailty interventions in older patients with gastric cancer, investigate predictive factors of frailty at the family level, and formulate targeted intervention strategies. Our research team simulated and intervened in the frailty heterogeneity trajectory of older patients with gastric cancer using the G-formula model [17]. The investigation revealed that family cohesion emerged as the second most important intervention factor for enhancing frailty outcomes. Our comparison of frailty interventions found a clear lack of programs focused on family cohesion, while those centered on nutritional support were far more common. Consequently, the formulation of intervention strategies targeting family cohesion is imperative to enhance the prognosis of frailty and to establish novel methodologies for the supplementation and optimization of frailty intervention strategies for older patients with gastric cancer.

Family cohesion is one of the dimensions of family function, reflecting the cohesion of emotional connections among family members [18]. The establishment of effective communication is identified as a key factor in fostering enhanced family cohesion [19]. The Satir Family Therapy Model [20] is predicated on the improvement of family communication, the catalyzing of change by integrating individual inner and interpersonal interactions, and the achievement of a functional, healthy, and satisfactory internal state of the family system [21]. In contrast to conventional family therapy models, this approach does not merely address the remediation of “symptoms”; rather, its fundamental objective is to facilitate the attainment of internal and external integration and consistency for individuals [22]. A multitude of studies have previously implemented this model with the objective of enhancing family cohesion [23]. In summary, the present study is guided by the Satir Family Therapy Model and focuses on family cohesion to construct a frailty intervention program for older patients with gastric cancer. The study explores the intervention effect on high-risk frailty older patients with gastric cancer and provides a new research perspective for supplementing and optimizing frailty intervention programs for this population.

sec.title: Study design and sample
sec.p: This was a non-randomized, time-based (sequential cohorts) controlled trial conducted in the Department of Gastrointestinal Surgery at a tertiary hospital in Jiangsu Province. Participants were assigned to the experimental or control group based on pre-specified admission time periods. Patients admitted between August and September 2024 were allocated to the experimental group, while those admitted between October and December 2024 were allocated to the control group. No patient or clinician choice was involved, and allocation was determined solely by calendar time. A 1-week washout period with no participant enrollment was implemented between these two consecutive enrollment phases (at the beginning of October 2024). This was to ensure no overlap in the hospital stay and follow-up schedule between the groups, thereby minimizing the risk of direct contamination. This non-random time-based allocation allowed separation of the usual-care and intervention phases, thereby reducing direct contact between participants from different study arms and helping to minimize contamination. To further safeguard against spillover, the intervention was delivered by a dedicated research team that was independent from the staff responsible for outcome assessment in the control group. Intervention-specific materials and training were restricted to the intervention phase and were not incorporated into routine hospital protocols during the subsequent control period. The ethical review process and trial registration procedures were completed prior to the enrollment of the first patient.

list-item.p: Patient inclusion criteria included the following: preoperative pathological evidence of gastric cancer with clear surgical indications; planned radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer; patients with a score of ≥ 0.385 on an online nomogram [11]; age ≥ 60 years; able to communicate verbally and in writing; able to understand and sign the informed consent form. Patient exclusion criteria included: preoperative receipt of radiotherapy or chemotherapy; combined with severe cardiac, hepatic, pulmonary, or renal dysfunction; physical dysfunction.

Family caregiver inclusion criteria included the following: age ≥ 18 years; spouse, child, or sibling of a high-risk frail patient; responsible for primary caregiving; conscious and able to communicate normally; voluntarily willing to participate in this study and sign an informed consent form. Family caregiver exclusion criteria included the following: previously received professional frailty care training for gastric cancer patients; in an employer-employee relationship.

sec.title: Development, training, and implementation of the intervention
sec.p: This intervention program was developed through theoretical research, literature review, and the Delphi expert consultation method. A total of 20 studies were included, comprising 10 descriptive studies, 6 qualitative studies, 3 reviews, and 1 mixed-methods study. The intervention components target the following areas: enhancing health literacy related to frailty, improving emotional cognition and management, identifying personal positive resources, fostering effective family communication, and developing family-based positive coping strategies. By applying an integrative review method, existing intervention strategies related to family support for frailty can be comprehensively and systematically integrated. Based on the theoretical framework of the Satir Family Therapy Model, which emphasizes that “improvements in family relationships must be built on the foundation of individual growth,” the subsequent intervention themes and strategies are arranged in the sequence of “professional knowledge learning—individual coping—family coping,” as detailed in Table 1.

sec.p: The intervention team consists of six members: a gastroenterological surgeon, a gastroenterological nurse manager, a gastroenterological nurse, a psychiatrist, and two nursing researchers. The nursing researchers were responsible for preparing the pre‑intervention work, implementing the intervention content for the intervention and control groups, and collecting baseline data (T0) on the day of admission. However, follow-up outcome assessments at T1 and T2 were conducted by independent trained research assistants who were blinded to group allocation and not involved in the intervention delivery. The remaining members assist in the research process (including disease treatment, psychological counseling, etc.). During hospitalization, face-to-face interventions were used, and after discharge, guided self-help interventions were provided to offer accessible intervention resources, breaking the constraints of time and space and promoting health equity. During follow-up, WeChat was used to supervise patients’ adherence to treatment and ensure the timely completion of homework assignments, effectively guaranteeing the implementation of the intervention.

To test the feasibility of the program, this study conducted a small-scale feasibility study. The recruitment rate was 100% (4/4); the retention rate was 75% (3/4), and the compliance rate was 50% (2/4). After communicating with the study subjects, the intervention content was adjusted: during formal recruitment, the significance of the project for the prognosis and rehabilitation of patients was explained in detail to patients and their family caregivers. The discussion began with conventional exercise and diet, helping patients and their family caregivers recognize the benefits of participating in the project. Then, combining the concept that the stomach is an emotional organ, the importance of good family cohesion in helping patients maintain a positive and optimistic attitude to cope with challenges was emphasized to reduce the dropout rate of study subjects during the intervention.

Based on expert consultation and feasibility study results, an intervention protocol draft was developed. Participants included gastric cancer patients aged 60 years and older who were scheduled for curative gastrectomy and their family caregivers. High-risk frail older patients with gastric cancer (identified through frailty screening and assessment using the frailty heterogeneity trajectory prediction model, a prior research outcome of the research team) and their family caregivers were selected. During hospitalization, two individual face-to-face interventions will be conducted, each lasting approximately 20 min. Post-discharge interventions will be delivered via online-guided self-help interventions for three consecutive weeks, once weekly. Researchers will conduct follow-up calls and collect feedback on intervention effectiveness, with each call lasting 10–15 min per person. The control group will receive standard frailty care; the experimental group will receive the family cohesion intervention in addition to standard frailty care. The specific intervention implementation draft is shown in the Additional file 1: Table S1.

sec.title: Features of the intervention
sec.p: This intervention program began upon the patient’s admission to the hospital, with one intervention session per week until the fourth week post-surgery, followed by follow-up until 1 month after the completion of the intervention. The program is characterized by a scientifically feasible intervention protocol and continuous intervention timing. The intervention program was designed to engage both patients and their family caregivers as an integrated participant unit. First, by enhancing cognitive awareness, the program helps patients and their family caregivers recognize the importance of frailty in post-surgery rehabilitation. Additionally, by improving family cohesion, the program aims to reverse frailty to some extent from psychological and social perspectives, thereby improving outcomes. Next, the Satir Iceberg metaphor was applied to help participants recognize the occurrence of their emotions, learn to accept them, identify their needs, and express them actively. Satir meditation techniques were used to empower participants, uncover their internal resources, and enhance their self-efficacy in addressing challenges. Satir communication posture techniques were employed to help participants observe their daily communication postures through visual body language, achieve consistency in communication through mind–body experiences, and truly achieve cohesion with one another. Finally, Satir positive coping beliefs were applied to introduce new ideas to participants, transform negative thinking patterns into positive thinking, experience immediate happiness in their surroundings, and form family-based positive coping strategies to address long-term rehabilitation challenges.

sec.title: Intervention fidelity monitoring
sec.p: To ensure intervention fidelity, several strategies were implemented. All interventionists completed standardized training based on a structured manual. A session-by-session fidelity checklist was used to document whether each component was delivered as intended. For in-hospital sessions, two investigators independently recorded session duration, content coverage, and participant engagement. For the post-discharge guided self-help sessions, completion was monitored through WeChat logs and weekly follow-up phone calls. A random 10% sample of sessions was independently reviewed by a senior researcher to assess adherence and consistency across interventionists.

sec.title: Standard care (control group)
sec.p: Participants in the control group received the standard frailty management pathway routinely provided in the Department of Gastric Surgery for older patients at high risk of frailty. Standard care consisted of a structured education program covering five core modules: (1) preoperative pre-rehabilitation guidance, (2) postoperative rehabilitation guidance, (3) home-based exercise guidance, (4) home-based dietary guidance, and (5) frailty prevention guidance.

The standard care program was delivered through face-to-face preoperative education by ward nurses during hospitalization, educational materials in the form of animated videos disseminated via WeChat during and after hospitalization, and routine post-discharge telephone follow-up conducted by department nurses to reinforce educational content and answer patient questions. This standard care pathway represents the usual level of care for this patient population.

Participants in the experimental group received all components of standard care, with the addition of a 5-time, once-weekly, therapist-led Satir Model-based family cohesion intervention involving fixed family members.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Researchers provided patients and their family caregivers with a detailed explanation of the study’s content prior to surgery. After obtaining explicit consent from patients and their family caregivers to participate in the study, their contact information was recorded for follow-up after discharge. Considering that most study participants had relatively low educational levels and economic status, and had high telephone usage and acceptance rates, this study adopted a combination of telephone and WeChat to ensure the progress of follow-up was smooth. Taking into account the feasibility and efficiency of follow-up, the study determined the follow-up time points in accordance with the requirements of the medical team, with the data collected at T0 (on the day of admission), T1 (at the end of the intervention, specifically at 4 weeks after surgery), and T2 (1 month after the completion of the intervention) (see Additional file 1: Fig. S1). Baseline (T0) data were collected by the nursing researchers at admission, whereas follow-up assessments at T1 and T2 were performed by independent blinded assessors.

sec.title: General information
sec.p: The high-risk population screening questionnaire was designed by the research team [11], including patient gender, age, educational level, marital status, family caregiver, place of residence, surgical history, tumor stage, weight, body mass index (BMI), number of comorbidities, grip strength, nutritional risk, depressive mood, social objective support, family cohesion, and number of health measurement tools.

sec.title: Frailty
sec.p: The Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI) was developed by COBBENS et al. [24] in 2010 and consists of three dimensions—physiological, psychological, and social—with a total of 15 items. The total frailty score ranges from 0 to 15, with physiological frailty scored from 0 to 8, psychological frailty from 0 to 4, and social frailty from 0 to 3. The cutoff scores for the total scale and the physical, psychological, and social dimensions are 5, 3, and 2, respectively. Higher scores indicate more severe frailty. The Cronbach’s α coefficient of the TFI frailty scale in the Chinese elderly population is 0.75, indicating good reliability and validity. The TFI was used to assess frailty in patients.

sec.title: Family cohesion
sec.p: Family Adaptability and Cohesion Evaluation Scales (FACESII-CV): Developed by Olson et al. [19] in 1982, this scale includes two dimensions—family cohesion and family adaptability—with a total of 30 items. It uses a Likert-type 1–5 rating scale, with higher scores indicating higher family cohesion and adaptability. In the Chinese population, the Cronbach’s α coefficient is > 0.60, indicating good reliability and validity. The family cohesion subscale from the FACESII-CV was used for the assessment of family cohesion in patients.

sec.title: Self-efficacy
sec.p: Cancer Self-Management Efficacy Scale (Strategies Used by People to Promote Health, SUPPH): Developed by Lev et al. [25] in 1996, it consists of 28 items, including three dimensions: positive attitudes, self-decision, and self-stress reduction. Higher scores indicate stronger self-management efficacy among patients. A Likert-type 1–5 rating scale was used, with Cronbach’s α coefficient ranging from 0.85 to 0.97, indicating good reliability and validity. The Cancer Self-Management Efficacy Scale was used to assess patients’ self-efficacy.

sec.title: Anxiety and depression
sec.p: Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS): This scale was developed by Zigmond AS et al. [26]. in 1983. It consists of 14 items, with 7 items assessing depressive symptoms and 7 items assessing anxiety symptoms. A total score > 7 indicates the possible presence of anxiety or depressive symptoms. The Cronbach’s α coefficient of this scale in the Chinese population is > 0.75, indicating good reliability and validity [27]. HADS was used to assess anxiety and depression in patients.

sec.title: Quality of life
sec.p: Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-General (FACT-G): This scale was developed by Cella et al. [28]. and includes 27 items across four dimensions: physical, functional, emotional, and social/family. The Cronbach’s α coefficient for each dimension is above 0.8. It uses a 5-point Likert scale, with each item scored from 0 to 4, and 5 items are reverse-scored. The total score is 108 points, with higher scores indicating better quality of life. FACT-G was used to assess the quality of life in patients.

All scales used in this study were validated Chinese versions. In the present sample, internal consistency reliability was acceptable to good, with Cronbach’s alpha coefficients ranging from 0.72 to 0.83 across the key measures.

sec.title: Sample size and power
sec.p: High-risk frail older patients with gastric cancer were recruited from the Department of Gastrointestinal Surgery of a tertiary hospital in Jiangsu Province from August 2024 to December 2024. In this study, frailty (assessed by the TFI score) was used as the primary outcome for sample size calculation. Referring to a previous intervention study that applied a family-based exercise program and reported a large effect on frailty (Cohen’s d = 0.77) [29], we assumed a comparable standardized effect size of 0.8 for our intervention. The sample size per group was calculated for a two-sided, two-independent-sample comparison of means using the following formula: n(per group) = 2 × S2 × (Z_{1-α/2} + Z_{1-β})2/d2, where S is the common standard deviation (set to 1 for a standardized effect size d), and Z_{1-α/2} and Z_{1-β} are the standard normal distribution values corresponding to the type I and II error rates, respectively. With a two-sided significance level (α) of 0.05 (Z_{1-α/2} = Z_{0.975} = 1.96) and a statistical power (1-β) of 90% (Z_{1-β} = Z_{0.90} = 1.28), the required sample size per group was calculated as follows: n = 2 × 12 × (1.96 + 1.28)2/0.82 = 2 × 1 × (3.24)2/0.64 = 2 × 10.4976/0.64 ≈ 32.8. Rounding up, 33 participants per group were needed. To account for potential loss to follow-up, we applied a conservative attrition rate of 15%, which is consistent with recent frailty intervention studies [29]. Although the registered protocol initially used a 20% assumption as a precautionary measure, the 15% rate was adopted later to reflect a more realistic estimate based on updated literature. The final sample size was therefore determined to be at least 2 × 33/0.85 = 77.6. Therefore, we aimed to recruit a minimum of 78 participants in total.

sec.title: Blinding
sec.p: To reduce the risk of measurement bias, a single-blind design was adopted. Baseline data were collected by the research team prior to intervention; blinding was not applicable at this stage because group allocation was already determined by admission time. For follow-up assessments, outcome assessors were blinded to participants’ group allocation. All outcome assessments at T1 and T2 were conducted via telephone by trained research staff who were not involved in intervention delivery. Assessors remained unaware of group assignment throughout the follow-up process and used standardized questionnaires and interview scripts to assess all outcome measures.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 27.0. First, descriptive statistical analysis was conducted on the baseline general characteristics of the two groups of patients. Continuous variables were examined for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Normally distributed continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and between-group comparisons were conducted using independent-samples t-tests. Non-normally distributed continuous variables were summarized as median [interquartile range, IQR], and between-group differences were assessed using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages and compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate.

To ensure that the study results better align with clinical practice, intention-to-treat analysis (ITT) was adopted. To avoid directly excluding missing values and affecting the statistical test efficacy, multiple imputation (MI) was used to fill in the missing values. An interpolation model was established based on the Fully Conditional Specification (FCS) method. This model incorporated group, time, age, sex, education status, TNM stage, preoperative nutritional risk, and all outcome variables (frailty, family cohesion, self-efficacy, anxiety, depression, quality of life) as predictors, with a total of 10 imputations performed. GEE analyses were performed separately on each of the 10 imputed datasets, and the resulting parameter estimates and standard errors were pooled using Rubin’s rules via the MI ANALYZE procedure in SPSS version 27.0. Analysis utilized MI-pooled results. To assess robustness of the interpolation results, a complete-case analysis was also performed as a sensitivity analysis. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) were used to analyze the effects of family cohesion intervention on outcome variables. The primary analysis using GEE with multiple imputation was based on the full intention-to-treat sample. For sensitivity analysis, a complete-case analysis was performed using data from the participants who provided outcome data at all three time points. GEE models assumed a Gaussian distribution with an identity link and an exchangeable working correlation structure. Robust (sandwich) standard errors were used. The model included time, group, and their interaction (Group*Time). To control for potential confounders, all GEE models adjusted for age, sex, education status, TNM stage, and preoperative nutritional risk, which were selected a priori based on clinical relevance and previous literature as potential confounders, particularly given the non-randomized, time-based allocation design. Multiple secondary outcomes were analyzed in an exploratory manner. No formal adjustment for multiple comparisons was applied; therefore, findings related to secondary outcomes should be interpreted with caution and considered hypothesis-generating. To examine whether baseline values moderate the intervention effect, age, sex, education status, TNM stage and preoperative nutritional risk were each tested as moderator variables to assess the three-way interaction effect of group*time*moderator. All statistical tests were performed with a two-sided P < 0.05 to determine statistical significance.

sec.title: Ethical considerations
sec.p: All patients signed informed consent before participation. This study approval was granted by the Ethics Committee of our university in China (no.: 2023–549) and registered by Chinese Clinical Trial Registry on April 7, 2024, with the registration number (ChiCTR2400082744), which confirmed that the registration was completed prior to enrollment of the first participant, indicating prospective registration.

sec.title: Adverse events monitoring
sec.p: All participants were actively monitored for adverse or unintended events throughout the intervention and follow-up period. Monitoring was conducted after each intervention contact and during follow-up telephone assessments at T1 and T2, using open-ended questions to identify any discomfort, distress, or negative experiences potentially related to study participation. No adverse or unintended events related to the intervention were reported during the study period. No adverse events associated with standard educational care were observed in the control group.

sec.title: Characteristics of participants
sec.p: A total of 79 patients (including 40 in the experimental group and 39 in the control group) were enrolled in this study. During the period, 2 were lost to follow-up in the experimental group, with 1 dying 1 month after intervention completion and 1 voluntarily withdrawing due to severe physical weakness 1 month after intervention completion. In the control group, 1 was lost to follow-up and could not be contacted 1 month after intervention completion, resulting in withdrawal from the study. A total of 76 participants who completed the five intervention sessions also provided outcome data at all three scheduled time points (T0, T1, and T2), with 38 in the experimental group and 38 in the control group, resulting in a total loss to follow-up rate of 3.8% (Fig. 1). Thus, the complete-case sample for sensitivity analysis comprised 76 participants. The primary GEE analyses presented below include all 79 participants via multiple imputation.

The experimental group included 40 older patients with gastric cancer at baseline, with an average age of (69.7 ± 5.17) years, including 13 females (32.5%) and 27 males (67.5%); the control group included 39 older patients with gastric cancer with an average age of (70.36 ± 5.24) years, including 10 females (25.6%) and 29 males (74.4%). There were no statistically significant differences between the two groups in terms of age, gender, educational level, marital status, family caregiver, place of residence, surgical history, tumor stage, body weight, BMI, grip strength, number of family-based health measurement tools, nutritional risk, objective social support, anxiety, depression, and high frailty risk (P > 0.05), indicating that the baseline characteristics of the two groups were comparable, as shown in Table 2.

sec.title: Comparison of frailty between the two groups
sec.p: Ten multiply imputed datasets were created. Diagnostic plots indicated adequate convergence. Sensitivity analyses showed that results from complete-case (n = 76) and MI-based GEE models (n = 79) were directionally consistent.

The GEE with covariate adjustment was used to assess the impact of the intervention on frailty. As shown in Table 3, the main effect of group was not statistically significant (β = − 1.932, 95% CI − 4.936 to 1.072, P = 0.207), indicating that group assignment alone did not exert an independent effect on frailty. The main effect of time did not reach significance (T1: β = − 0.179, P = 0.474; T2: β = −0.621, P = 0.053), although a downward trend was observed. However, the group by time interaction was significant at both time points (T1: β = − 0.646, 95% CI − 1.214 to − 0.077, P = 0.026; T2: β = − 0.859, 95% CI − 1.654 to − 0.065, P = 0.034). This indicates that, compared with the control group, the experimental group was associated with greater improvement in frailty at T1 and T2, with the magnitude of between-group differences increasing over time (Fig. 2). None of the covariates showed significant associations with frailty (all P > 0.05). Pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means (EMMs) of frailty were provided in Additional file 1: Table S2.

sec.title: Comparison of family cohesion between the two groups
sec.p: Table 3 shows that the main effect of group on family cohesion is not significant (β = 1.434, 95% CI −0.589 to 3.457, P = 0.165). The main effect of time also did not reach statistical significance (T1: β = 0.487, P = 0.187; T2: β = 0.431, P = 0.414). In contrast, the group by time interaction was significant at both time points (T1: β = 1.513, 95% CI 0.580 to 2.446, P = 0.001; T2: β = 3.194, 95% CI 1.769 to 4.619, P < 0.001). These findings indicate that the experimental group showed a greater increase in family cohesion at T1 and T2 compared with the control group, with the improvement continuing to strengthen over time (Fig. 2). Additionally, age (β = − 0.083, P = 0.001) and educational level (≥ College: β = −1.787, P = 0.006) showed independent associations with family cohesion. Pairwise comparisons of EMMs of family cohesion are provided in Additional file 1: Table S3.

sec.title: Comparison of self-efficacy between the two groups of patients
sec.p: Table 3 indicates that the main effect of group on self-efficacy was not significant (β = 0.428, 95% CI − 4.878 to 5.734, P = 0.874). A significant main effect of time was observed (T1: β = 2.051, P < 0.001; T2: β = 2.403, P < 0.001), suggesting that self-efficacy was significantly associated with improvement over time across the sample. Importantly, the interaction was significant at both time points (T1: β = 1.699, 95% CI 0.188 to 3.209, P = 0.028; T2: β = 4.212, 95% CI 2.217 to 6.208, P < 0.001). This indicates that the experimental group showed greater gains in self-efficacy at T1 and T2 than the control group, with effects amplified at follow-up (Fig. 2). Female sex, lower educational attainment, and TNM stage II were independently associated with lower self-efficacy (all P < 0.05). Pairwise comparisons of EMMs of self-efficacy were provided in Additional file 1: Table S4.

sec.title: Comparison of anxiety between the two groups of patients
sec.p: Table 3 shows that the main effect of group on anxiety was not significant (β = 0.363, 95% CI − 0.320 to 1.047, P = 0.298). The main effect of time exhibited a phased change: anxiety significantly increased at the end of the intervention (T1: β = 0.872, 95% CI 0.501 to 1.242, P < 0.001), while anxiety levels decreased but did not reach significance one month post-intervention (T2: β = − 0.226, 95% CI − 0.585 to 0.133, P = 0.218). Notably, the group by time interaction was significant at both T1 and T2 (T1: β = − 0.672, 95% CI − 1.321 to − 0.023, P = 0.043; T2: β = − 0.762, 95% CI − 1.313 to − 0.211, P = 0.007), indicating that the intervention buffered anxiety trends at both time points: significantly attenuating the rise in anxiety at T1 and promoting its decline at T2, with effects superior to the control group, as shown in Fig. 2. Age showed an independent positive association with anxiety (β = 0.028, P = 0.012). Pairwise comparisons of EMMs of anxiety were provided in Additional file 1: Table S5.

sec.title: Comparison of depression between the two groups of patients
sec.p: Table 3 shows that the main effect of group on depression was not significant (β = −0.378, 95% CI − 1.064 to 0.308, P = 0.280). The time effect was not significant at T1 (β = 0.308, P = 0.181), but a significant improvement was observed at T2 (β = − 0.600, 95% CI − 0.949 to − 0.251, P = 0.001). Notably, the group by time interaction was significant at both time points (T1: β = − 0.633, 95% CI −1.231 to − 0.034, P = 0.038; T2: β = − 0.812, 95% CI − 1.339 to − 0.286, P = 0.003). This indicates that greater reductions in depression were observed in the experimental group compared with the control group at both T1 and T2 (Fig. 2). Sex, educational status, and nutritional risk were also associated with depression (P < 0.05). Pairwise comparisons of EMMs of depression were provided in Additional file 1: Table S6.

sec.title: Comparison of quality of life between the two groups
sec.p: Table 3 demonstrates that the main effect of group on quality of life (QoL) was not significant (β = 1.020, 95% CI − 0.917 to 2.957, P = 0.302). A bidirectional time effect was observed: QoL decreased at T1 (β = − 2.923, P < 0.001) but improved significantly at T2 (β = 1.000, 95% CI 0.015 to 1.985, P = 0.047). Importantly, the group by time interaction was significant at T2 (β = 4.843, 95% CI 3.404 to 6.281, P < 0.001), suggesting that the intervention was significantly associated with improvement in QoL at follow-up, exceeding that of the control group (Fig. 2). Female participants had significantly lower QoL (β = − 2.329, P = 0.008). Pairwise comparisons of EMMs of quality of life were provided in Additional file 1: Table S7.

sec.title: Moderation analysis
sec.p: Moderation analyses were conducted by adding three-way interaction terms (group*time*moderator) for five baseline covariates (age, sex, education status, TNM stage, and preoperative nutritional risk). Overall, most moderation effects were not significant, suggesting consistent temporal changes in intervention effects across patients with different baseline characteristics. Only a few interaction terms reached statistical significance: age significantly moderated self-efficacy (T1vsT0), depression (T1vsT0, T2vsT0), and quality of life (T1vsT0), with greater age associated with larger intervention-induced improvements. Educational status moderated intervention effects at specific time points for certain outcomes (frailty, self-efficacy, anxiety, and quality of life). Patients with TNM stage III or higher exhibited a significant negative moderation effect on quality of life improvement (T1 vs T0), suggesting that the quality of life gains from the intervention were smaller in patients with more advanced TNM staging. All other moderation effects (including gender and nutritional risk) failed to reach statistical significance. The pooled β, SE, and 95% CI for all three-way interaction terms are presented in Additional file 1: Table S8.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study developed a frailty intervention program centered on family cohesion based on the Satir Family Therapy Model and validated its effectiveness in improving multidimensional outcomes among older gastric cancer patients. Results demonstrated that the intervention not only was significantly associated with improvement in frailty and family cohesion but also exhibited significant group by time interaction effects on outcome measures including self-efficacy, anxiety, depression, and quality of life, suggesting the intervention provides stable and comprehensive potential benefits. First, regarding frailty and family cohesion, this study found that the experimental group was associated with significantly better frailty and family cohesion scores at both T1 and T2 compared with the control group, with the magnitude of between-group differences increasing over time. This suggests that family cohesion-based interventions may be associated with improvements in family cohesion and sustained reductions in frailty. Potential mechanisms underlying these associations may involve changes in family interaction patterns and emotional connectedness. Enhanced family cohesion may be associated with reduced communication conflicts and more consistent coping strategies between patients and family caregivers. In addition, greater family cohesion may be associated with increased willingness for social participation and adherence to rehabilitation activities, which could partly explain the strengthening of the observed associations over time. The sustained decline in frailty post-intervention aligns closely with the philosophy in Satir Family Therapy Model of facilitating deep, systemic change [20, 22]. Furthermore, these findings align with prior studies applying the Satir Family Therapy Model to improve family functioning and individual health outcomes among cancer patients [30, 31], further validating the theoretical framework's efficacy and applicability in oncology rehabilitation—particularly for frail older populations.

Regarding self-efficacy, this study found significant interaction effects at both T1 and T2, with the experimental group showing a greater increase than the control group. Potential explanations for this association may relate to components of the Satir Model, which emphasize authentic self-expression and role clarification within family interactions. Such processes may be associated with increased perceived support and affirmation from family members, which, in turn, could be linked to greater confidence in addressing rehabilitation-related challenges [32].

In terms of emotional states, this study found that both anxiety and depression exhibited significant group by time interaction effects. Depression decreased significantly following intervention and showed a sustained improvement trend over time. The reason may be the “iceberg metaphor” technique of the Satir Family Therapy Model, which helps patients recognize suppressed emotional needs and rebuild psychological security through family emotional expression [33]. Anxiety exhibited a delayed intervention effect, with both groups showing a certain degree of increase in anxiety levels at T1, which began to decline only at T2. This trend aligns with the typical psychological trajectory during the postoperative recovery process for gastric cancer. The 4-week postoperative period (T1) typically represents a “peak period” of physical and psychological stress for patients, often characterized by significant physical discomfort, dietary restrictions, reduced physical capacity, and concerns about uncertain prognosis [34]. While family cohesion-based interventions at this stage can provide emotional support, they struggle to fully counteract the anxiety stemming from postoperative physiological burdens. However, the Satir Model’s emphasis on emotion recognition, effective expression, and supportive communication helps patients reduce emotional distress during high-stress periods, resulting in a smaller increase in the experimental group. As postoperative recovery enters a stable phase (T2), the intervention’s effects, including enhanced family support consistency, improved communication quality, and strengthened family system functioning, gradually manifest. These psychological benefits may accumulate over time, and may be associated with a significant decrease in anxiety at T2.

The trajectory of quality of life changes also revealed a delayed intervention effect. At the completion of the intervention, specifically at the 4-week postoperative mark, patients remained in the transitional phase of the early postoperative period. Their diets had not yet returned to normal, and physical exertion from the surgery left them insufficiently strong to perform routine household tasks [35]. A return to preoperative daily activities showed a difficult pattern in the short term, resulting in a decline in quality of life compared to baseline levels. However, the quality of life in the experimental group significantly surpassed the control group at the 1-month follow-up. Once patients mastered meditation empowerment and positive coping strategies, their self-management efficacy improved, thereby increasing nutritional intake and daily activity capabilities. Notably, after a brief decline in quality of life from T0 to T1, the experimental group showed a significant increase from T1 to T2, which may reflect sustained improvement during the home-based recovery period.

Additionally, moderation analysis revealed limited moderating effects of age, education status, and TNM stage on certain outcomes, suggesting that intervention effects may vary across different subgroups. This implies that future clinical implementation should design personalized modules based on population heterogeneity, such as providing more frequent or intensive interventions for patients with lower education status or higher tumor stages.

The theoretical breakthrough of this study lies in reconstructing the frailty intervention paradigm. Traditional pre-rehabilitation programs focus on the individualized intervention of exercise-nutrition [36, 37]. This study, however, introduces the “family system” as a fourth dimension, establishing an “individual-family-environment” intervention model. The application of communication stances from the Satir Model transformed family caregivers from passive observers into active agents of change [38], addressing the “role ambiguity” challenge in previous family interventions. This intervention represents a progressive journey from “self-growth” to “family growth”. Throughout this process, patients and family caregivers progressively acquire the knowledge and skills essential for long-term disease rehabilitation. More importantly, they develop a positive family functional pattern characterized by active interaction and mutual support. Family caregivers not only provide daily care but also play a pivotal role in stimulating patients' “active health motivation” through emotional support and skill assistance. This empowerment of caregivers enables them to deliver stable, sustained high-quality support [39], creating a mutually nurturing positive cycle between patients and caregivers—a crucial safeguard for the intervention’s lasting effectiveness.

This study has some limitations. First, this study included only 79 older gastric cancer survivors with high-risk frailty, and the final sample size was 76. The relatively small sample size may compromise the generalizability and representativeness of the findings. The follow-up duration was short, which may be insufficient for evaluating the long-term effects of the family cohesion intervention on frailty and other outcomes. Future research should expand the sample size and extend the follow-up period to observe the sustained impacts of family cohesion interventions on these key indicators, thereby providing evidence for the development of sustainable intervention strategies. Second, this study adopted a non-randomized control design rather than a fully randomized controlled trial, potentially introducing confounding factors. Although allocation was determined by time period rather than patient preference, differences may exist between the two groups in terms of disease severity, motivation, or family support. Despite covariate adjustments, the non-randomized, time-based allocation may introduce residual confounding and secular trend bias, thereby preventing definitive confirmation of causal inferences. Furthermore, although there is a one-week washout period, the sequential enrollment with the experimental phase preceding the control phase introduces a risk of historical bias or unmeasured temporal effects. We implemented measures to isolate the intervention, but there is still a possibility of unobserved bias, which could affect the estimates in either direction. This means that the observed effect sizes could be either overestimated or underestimated, and caution is warranted when interpreting the findings. Finally, the study population was restricted to participants recruited from only one hospital, limiting the geographical diversity of the sample and potentially constraining the generalizability of the findings. To enhance external validity and promote the broader applicability of results, future studies should employ multicenter RCT designs and include patients from diverse regions and healthcare institutions.

In summary, this study precisely targeted “family cohesion” as the intervention focus. By developing a frailty intervention program based on the Satir Family Therapy model—promoting knowledge sharing, improving family communication, strengthening emotional bonds, and empowering primary caregivers—this program ultimately established a supportive family interaction system that effectively alleviated frailty in older gastric cancer patients across multiple dimensions, suggesting potential benefits. This provides crucial theoretical foundations and practical pathways for establishing a “hospital-to-home” continuum of care system.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In summary, this study suggests that the frailty intervention focused on family cohesion may be associated with improvements in family cohesion, frailty, self-efficacy, anxiety, depression, and quality of life among high-risk frail older patients with gastric cancer. In addition, the findings provide preliminary insights and references for future empirical research on frailty interventions from a multidimensional perspective, and signal the potential value of developing more scientific, effective, and comprehensive frailty intervention systems for older patients with gastric cancer.
